_draft.source_quote: any person who, by putting his name on the product or using a trade mark or other distinguishing mark in relation to the product, has held himself out to be the producer of the product

subject: Tort
title: Who can sue in private nuisance: an interest in land is required (Hunter, confirmed in Fearn v Tate)
scenario: Mrs Okafor owns the freehold of a house in England and lives there with her adult son, Samuel, who has no tenancy or other legal interest in the property and lives there with her permission. A recycling plant opens next door and, for several months, produces constant loud noise and strong smells that substantially interfere with the use and enjoyment of the house. Both Mrs Okafor and Samuel want to sue the plant operator in private nuisance.
stem: Which of the following best describes who can sue in private nuisance?

options.A: Mrs Okafor can sue, but Samuel cannot, because only a person with an interest in the affected land can sue in private nuisance.
options.B: Both can sue, because each of them lives in the house and suffers the interference.
options.C: Only Samuel can sue, because he is the person who suffers the interference most, being at home all day.
options.D: Neither can sue in private nuisance, because noise and smells affecting a neighbourhood can only be a public nuisance.
options.E: Both can sue, but Samuel can recover only for any personal injury he suffers.

explanation: Private nuisance is a tort against land: it protects the use and enjoyment of land, and the claim belongs to the person with an interest in the affected land. In Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd [1997] AC 655 the House of Lords held that only a person with a proprietary interest in the land (or exclusive possession of it) can sue. The Supreme Court confirmed this in Fearn v Board of Trustees of the Tate Gallery [2023] UKSC 4. Mrs Okafor, as freehold owner in occupation, has the necessary interest and can sue for the substantial interference with the use and enjoyment of her house. Samuel, a family member living there by permission with no interest in the land, cannot sue in private nuisance, however much the noise and smells affect him. Damages in private nuisance are assessed by reference to the diminution in the amenity value of the land, rather than the personal discomfort of each occupier.

why_wrong.B: Hunter rejected the argument that mere occupation of a home is enough; an interest in the land is required.
why_wrong.C: Samuel has no interest in the land, so he cannot sue however much he personally suffers.
why_wrong.D: Interference with the use and enjoyment of a neighbour's land is classic private nuisance, whether or not others are affected.
why_wrong.E: Samuel has no standing in private nuisance at all, and personal injury is not recoverable in private nuisance in any event.

key_rule: Only a person with an interest in the affected land (or exclusive possession) can sue in private nuisance; licensees such as family members cannot.
authority: Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd [1997] AC 655, confirmed in Fearn v Board of Trustees of the Tate Gallery [2023] UKSC 4

_draft.spec_topic: Nuisance: public and private nuisance
_draft.source_quote: because the interest protected by the tort of private nuisance is the use and enjoyment of land, only a person with a legal interest in the land can sue.
_draft.uncertainty: Hunter itself was not fetched; the rule is taken from the Supreme Court's account in Fearn. The statement in option E that personal injury is not recoverable in private nuisance rests on Hunter/Transco, not on a fetched passage.

subject: Tort
title: Defences in private nuisance: coming to the nuisance and planning permission (Coventry v Lawrence)
scenario: Six years ago, Thornfield Raceway Ltd began holding motocross events on its land in rural England, with planning permission for that use. Two years ago, Ms Adeyemi bought a farmhouse nearby and moved in, using it as her home, as previous owners had done. The noise from the events substantially interferes with the use and enjoyment of her home and, the court finds, amounts to a nuisance. Thornfield argues that (1) Ms Adeyemi came to the nuisance, knowing about the events when she bought, and (2) its activities have planning permission.
stem: Which of the following best describes Thornfield's arguments?

options.A: Argument (1) is a complete defence, because a claimant who buys property knowing of an existing nuisance is taken to have accepted it.
options.B: Argument (2) is a complete defence, because planning permission authorises the activity in the same way as statutory authority.
options.C: Thornfield has acquired a right to make the noise by prescription, because the events had taken place before Ms Adeyemi bought her house.
options.D: Neither argument provides a defence, although the court has a discretion whether to grant an injunction or to award damages instead.
options.E: Neither argument provides a defence, and the court must grant an injunction stopping the events once a nuisance is established.

explanation: In Coventry v Lawrence [2014] UKSC 13 the Supreme Court confirmed that it is no defence to a nuisance claim that the claimant came to the nuisance, at least where the claimant uses her property for essentially the same purpose as her predecessors did before the nuisance began. Ms Adeyemi uses the farmhouse as a home, as before. The Court also held that the mere fact that the activity has the benefit of planning permission is normally of no assistance to the defendant in a claim by a neighbour complaining of noise or other loss of amenity; planning permission is not equivalent to statutory authority. Neither argument therefore defeats the claim. As to remedy, the Court emphasised that whether to grant an injunction or award damages in lieu is a matter for the court's discretion, which should not be fettered by a mechanical application of the Shelfer criteria; planning permission may be relevant to that discretion.

why_wrong.A: Coming to the nuisance has for over 180 years been held to be no defence.
why_wrong.B: Planning permission is not statutory authority and is normally of no assistance as a defence to a nuisance claim.
why_wrong.C: A prescriptive right requires at least 20 years' actionable nuisance; these events have taken place for only six years.
why_wrong.E: An injunction is a discretionary remedy; the court may award damages in lieu instead.

key_rule: Coming to the nuisance is no defence, planning permission normally does not assist a defendant in nuisance, and the choice between injunction and damages in lieu is discretionary.
authority: Coventry v Lawrence [2014] UKSC 13

_draft.spec_topic: Nuisance: remedies (damages and injunctions) and defences
_draft.source_quote: For over 180 years it has been assumed and authoritatively stated to be the law that it is no defence for a defendant to a nuisance claim to argue that the claimant came to the nuisance.
_draft.uncertainty: The planning permission quote ('normally of no assistance to the defendant') was also verified in the same judgment. The 20-year prescription period and the Shelfer discretion are stated from Lawrence generally; reviewer may wish to confirm those passages.

subject: Tort
title: Rylands v Fletcher: strict liability for property damage but not personal injury
scenario: Fenbrook Chemicals Ltd stores large quantities of a highly corrosive industrial solvent in tanks on its site in England, an extraordinary use of land carrying an increased danger to neighbours if the solvent escapes. Despite Fenbrook having taken all reasonable care, a tank fails and the solvent escapes onto the neighbouring farm owned and occupied by Mr Lindqvist. It ruins crops and contaminates his land. Mr Lindqvist also suffers burns to his hands when trying to stop the flow. Damage of this kind from an escape was foreseeable.
stem: Which of the following best describes Mr Lindqvist's claim under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher?

options.A: He can recover for the damage to his land and crops and for his burns, without proving negligence.
options.B: He can recover nothing, because Fenbrook took all reasonable care, and Rylands liability depends on proof of negligence.
options.C: He can recover for the damage to his land and crops without proving negligence, but not for his burns, which cannot be claimed under Rylands.
options.D: He can recover for his burns but not for the damage to his land and crops, which is pure economic loss.
options.E: He can recover nothing, because storing chemicals on industrial premises is an ordinary use of land.

explanation: Under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher, as restated in Transco plc v Stockport MBC and summarised in Stannard v Gore [2012] EWCA Civ 1248, an occupier who brings or keeps on its land an exceptionally dangerous or mischievous thing in extraordinary or unusual circumstances is liable, without proof of negligence, for damage to a neighbouring occupier's property interest caused by the thing's escape, subject to limited defences. Fenbrook kept large quantities of a corrosive solvent in a way the facts describe as an extraordinary use carrying increased danger; the solvent escaped onto neighbouring land and caused foreseeable damage. Mr Lindqvist, as owner-occupier, can therefore recover for the damage to his land and crops even though Fenbrook took all reasonable care. However, Rylands is a species of nuisance protecting interests in land, so a claim for death or personal injury cannot be brought under it. His burns must be claimed in negligence, which would require proof of fault.

why_wrong.A: Personal injury is not recoverable under Rylands v Fletcher, which protects rights in or enjoyment of land.
why_wrong.B: Rylands liability is strict; the claimant need not prove negligence.
why_wrong.D: Physical damage to land and crops is damage to property, not pure economic loss, and it is what Rylands protects; the burns are not recoverable under it.
why_wrong.E: The facts state that this storage was an extraordinary use carrying increased danger, so it was not an ordinary use of land.

key_rule: An occupier who keeps an exceptionally dangerous thing in extraordinary circumstances is strictly liable for foreseeable damage to a neighbour's property from its escape, but not for personal injury.
authority: Rylands v Fletcher (1868) LR 3 HL 330; Transco plc v Stockport MBC [2003] UKHL 61; Stannard v Gore [2012] EWCA Civ 1248

_draft.spec_topic: Nuisance: the rule in Rylands v Fletcher
_draft.source_quote: Second, the claim cannot include a claim for death or personal injury, since such a claim does not relate to any right in or enjoyment of land.
_draft.uncertainty: Transco itself was not fetched; its principles are taken from the extracts quoted in Stannard v Gore.
